project_scope.selection_mode: San Marcos River Heteranthera-first aquatic lesson
project_scope.note: Current local lesson is intentionally species-centered because the family is morphologically broader than the single canonical anchor.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Begin with the aquatic habit, then inspect the inflorescence and flower: Heteranthera dubia has narrow submerged foliage and a solitary yellow flower with three fertile stamens; Pontederia cordata has emergent leaves and a dense flowering spike; Pontederia crassipes forms floating rosettes with often swollen petioles. Confirm using reproductive structures rather than leaf shape or color alone.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Aquatic or wetland monocots; leaf form varies widely across the family.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Perianth commonly 6-parted; floral symmetry and stamen number vary by genus. Heteranthera dubia has a yellow salverform flower with three stamens.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Fruit differs by genus: Heteranthera dubia produces a capsule; Pontederia cordata develops a one-seeded indehiscent fruit enclosed by persistent floral tissue; Pontederia crassipes can produce a many-seeded capsule. Do not generalize the Heteranthera fruit or seed morphology to the whole family.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Do not generalize the narrow grasslike leaves or yellow flower to all Pontederiaceae—those are Heteranthera traits.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: Heteranthera dubia is a memorable family doorway because the grasslike aquatic foliage suddenly produces a bright yellow flower with unusual left/right reproductive handedness.

steps.title: 1 · Start with the aquatic habit
steps.look_for: Thin linear leaves on a submerged or procumbent aquatic plant.
steps.why_it_matters: The plant can look grasslike until it flowers.

steps.title: 2 · Find the solitary yellow flower
steps.look_for: One yellow flower with a long tube rising above the foliage.
steps.why_it_matters: The reproductive structure immediately breaks the grasslike illusion.

steps.title: 3 · Count three stamens
steps.look_for: Three equal stamens plus the style inside the 6-part flower.
steps.why_it_matters: This is a strong local genus/species confirmation.

steps.title: 4 · Compare mirror-image flowers
steps.look_for: Style and anthers positioned as left/right mirror images between flowers.
steps.why_it_matters: A powerful morphology lesson, even though it should not be the sole ID character.

steps.title: 5 · Check ovary position against tape-grass
steps.photo_role: matched Pontederiaceae flower side/section versus Vallisneria female flower side/section
steps.look_for: In a verified flower side view or dissection, trace the perianth insertion: BELOW the superior ovary in Pontederiaceae, ABOVE the inferior ovary in the female Vallisneria flower. A flower-face photograph cannot establish this.
steps.why_it_matters: Superior versus inferior ovary separates these otherwise confusable aquatic monocot families; Vallisneria also has detached floating male flowers and a coiling female stalk.

comparisons.title: Pontederiaceae vs grasslike aquatics
comparisons.rule: Linear leaves alone are misleading. The showy 6-part flower and capsule place Heteranthera far from Poaceae.

comparisons.title: Route local Pontederiaceae genera
comparisons.rule: Solitary yellow flower with three stamens and narrow aquatic leaves suggests Heteranthera dubia. A dense emergent spike suggests Pontederia cordata; floating rosettes with often inflated petioles suggest Pontederia crassipes. Confirm flowers and fruit.

comparisons.title: Pontederiaceae vs Potamogetonaceae
comparisons.rule: In narrow-leaved submerged aquatics, inspect the leaf base: compare the Heteranthera sheath with Potamogeton stipules. Confirm the showy six-part Heteranthera flower versus reduced pondweed spike flowers; leaf shape alone is not enough.

comparisons.title: Pontederiaceae vs Commelinaceae — floral parts
comparisons.rule: Compare six petaloid perianth lobes in Pontederiaceae with three distinct sepals and three petals in Commelinaceae. Heteranthera dubia has three fertile stamens; Commelina commonly has three fertile stamens plus three staminodes. Both families generally have superior ovaries, so ovary position alone does not separate them.

comparisons.title: Pontederiaceae vs Hydrocharitaceae — ovary position and aquatic flowers
comparisons.rule: Do not use aquatic habit or ribbonlike leaves alone. In the local Pontederiaceae, inspect a flower side view: the ovary is SUPERIOR (the perianth arises below it); Heteranthera dubia has a conspicuous bisexual six-part flower and a capsule, while Pontederia cordata has a many-flowered spike and a one-seeded indehiscent fruit enclosed by persistent floral tissue. In the local Hydrocharitaceae representative Vallisneria, the female flower has an INFERIOR ovary (perianth above it); detached male flowers float at the surface, and the long female peduncle coils after fertilization. These floating-male and coiling-peduncle traits describe Vallisneria, not every Hydrocharitaceae. PHOTO HANDOFF: matched, anatomically verified side/section views of a Pontederiaceae flower and a Vallisneria female flower showing the perianth insertion relative to the ovary, plus a Vallisneria male/female surface-pollination sequence. Existing Heteranthera flower frame jvid-Hr3nBxvgCv4-016 (Joey Santore, private-study only; public reuse not cleared) is a source reference, NOT proof of ovary position or a licensed public comparison image. Arrow positions annotation_pending until actual pixels/sections are checked.

visual_lesson.caveat: Use the Heteranthera lesson as a local anchor, not a universal visual definition of broad Pontederiaceae.
